core: Three time frames: present, past, and future; most tenses built with helping verbs
Four aspects: simple, continuous (progressive), perfect, perfect continuous, each with an example in one tense
Helping verbs be, have, and will in tense formation
Regular -ed past forms vs high-frequency irregulars (go/went/gone, see/saw/seen, take/took/taken, eat/ate/eaten)
Present simple vs present continuous (habits and general facts vs actions in progress now)
Past simple vs present perfect (finished time vs time up to now / connection to the present)
Future basics: will vs be going to
Common learner tense errors with corrections

Verb forms as building blocks (base, -s, -ing, past, past participle)

claims.claim: English has three time frames — present, past, and future — and only two tenses are conveyed by the verb alone (present sing, past sang); most English tenses are marked by auxiliaries.
The perfect tenses are formed by adding an auxiliary (have/has/had) to the past participle, and the continuous tenses are formed with be plus the -ing form.

The present perfect designates action which began in the past but continues into the present or whose effect still continues, while the simple past locates action in finished time; the classic pair is 'Betty has taught for ten years' (still teaches today) versus 'Betty taught for ten years' (no longer teaches).

The present simple is used for permanent facts, general truths, habits, and routines, while the present continuous is used for temporary situations and actions happening now; some verbs (know, like, understand) are not normally used in the continuous.

Regular verbs form their past tense and past participle by adding -ed; irregular verbs such as go, see, take, and eat have their own past and past-participle forms that learners must memorize as vocabulary items.
Will (and shall) are used to make predictions, to state facts about the future, and to announce decisions and offers at the moment of speaking.

Be going to (be going to + base form) is used for future plans and intentions whose decision has already been made, and for predictions the speaker has present evidence for; will is used when stating something with certainty.

The past simple is used for definite time in the past, usually with past time expressions such as yesterday, two weeks ago, last year, and in 1995; the present perfect is used for time up to now, with expressions such as today, this year, since, and already.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How many English tenses are there? Some grammars count exactly two because only present and past are marked on the verb itself; the Purdue OWL presents six basic tenses and notes that as many as thirty are marked by auxiliaries.
positions: Exactly two tenses (present, past), with all other time meanings expressed through auxiliary constructions
Six basic tenses (simple present, present perfect, simple past, past perfect, future, future perfect), with further aspect combinations recognized
Cambridge grammar describes individual constructions (present simple, present continuous, past simple, present perfect, future forms) without asserting a single total count
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson follows the OWL six-basic-tense framework and states plainly that only present and past are shown by the verb alone, so both descriptions agree in substance; no count dispute is asserted.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Will versus be going to overlap heavily in future meaning; some teaching materials present them as strict alternatives.
positions: Cambridge notes will and be going to are often used in similar ways, with will for absolute certainty and going to to emphasize a decision or present evidence
Strict-alternative rules (e.g., 'going to = plans, will = predictions') appear in learner materials
Both constructions are acceptable in many sentences, with speaker emphasis deciding
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents both as workable in many situations and teaches the emphasis distinction from Cambridge: evidence or a decision already made points to going to; an on-the-spot decision or a plain prediction points to will.

sourceRecords.title: Present perfect simple or past simple? — Cambridge Dictionary Grammar
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B. Read live on 2026-08-21 (HTTP 200). Supports: past simple for definite time in the past, usually with past time expressions such as yesterday, two weeks ago, last year, in 1995; present perfect for time up to now, i.e., events that took place in the past but connect with the present, often with today, this year, since, in the last six months; the not-forms I haven't seen her since January 1995 vs I didn't see her since January 1995. Proprietary reference; facts only.

sourceRecords.title: Future: will and shall — Cambridge Dictionary Grammar
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B. Read live on 2026-08-21 (HTTP 200). Supports: will and shall for predictions and statements of fact about the future (There will be strong winds tomorrow); announcing decisions and offers at the moment of speaking (I'll have large); shall as a more formal alternative with I and we. Proprietary reference; facts only.

sourceRecords.title: Future: be going to (I am going to work) — Cambridge Dictionary Grammar
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B. Read live on 2026-08-21 (HTTP 200). Supports: be going to + base form for future plans and intentions whose decision is already made (I'm going to look for a new place to live next month) and for predictions that are certain or evidenced now (It's going to snow again soon, with visible clouds); the will/going-to comparison (will for certainty, going to to emphasize a decision or present evidence); gonna as the informal spoken form. Proprietary reference; facts only.
